paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (a minor Appellant), citizen of Albania and Turkey, appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated April 1, 2019, rejecting her claim for refugee protection. A designated representative, XXXX XXXX was appointed as the designated representative for the minor Appellant XXXX at the RPD hearing and he remains the designated representative for XXXX before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). XXXX is represented by the same counsel that represented her and her family at the RPD hearing. The Minister's Representative participated before the RPD through the submission of documents but has not participated in this appeal.
The determinative issue in this appeal is whether the RPD erred in its findings in regard to the minor Appellant risk of harm or persecution in Albania.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).2 BACKGROUND

The Appellant, a minor aged three, lived in Albania with her parents and sibling prior to coming to Canada to seek refugee status. In its reasons for decision the RPD determined that the Appellant's parents and sibling were found to have refugee claims against Turkey where they are citizens. The parents, who had been living and teaching in Albania with the Hizmet movement on temporary visas for some years, feared persecution in Turkey if they should return. Their refugee claims in Canada were accepted by the RPD as well founded. However, the RPD found that the minor Appellant XXXX, is a citizen of both Albania and Turkey and that she had not established a case for persecution or harm in Albania and her claim was denied on that basis. The RPD Decision

As noted above, the RPD found the Appellant's family, who are citizens of Turkey and no other country, to be Convention refugees.3 However the RPD found that the Appellant, who is also a citizen of Albania, would not be persecuted or harmed in Albania and therefore that she is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Appellant's Argument

The Appellant's counsel argues on behalf of the Appellant that the RPD erred in its treatment of the documentary evidence in regard to conditions in Albania for the supporters of the Turkish Hizmet movement and by extension, their families. I will deal with the Appellant's arguments in more detail below. New Evidence and Oral Hearing
The Appellant's counsel has submitted no new evidence and does not request an oral hearing before the RAD.

With respect to questions of fact and mixed fact and law, I have applied the standard of correctness as per Huruglica.4 When reviewing the RPD decision, I am required to independently determine whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, fact or mixed fact and law. I may defer to the RPD's credibility assessment of oral testimony, if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage in the circumstances. Reasons will be provided in my analysis if I find that the RPD had meaningful advantage.

It is the persons claiming refugee protection and not the RPD or the RAD that bears the onus of establishing the need for refugee protection. It is the responsibility of the RPD or the RAD to consider the applicable case law and weigh the documentary and testimonial evidence and to draw conclusions as to whether the evidence is sufficient to establish the Appellants' allegations. In this case, the RPD panel did not find that the minor Appellant had provided sufficient evidence to establish that she would be persecuted upon returning to Albania.

In its reasons for decision the RPD panel stated the following in regard to the minor Appellant: The Albanian minor Claimant's BOC form makes no allegations of risk. During the proceeding, counsel indicated that the Albanian minor Claimant faces a risk in Albania due to her membership in the Hizmet movement. The adult Claimants were asked if there was any risk to the Albanian minor Claimant in Albania and the male Claimant testified that the Albanian minor Claimant is very young therefore she cannot be in Albania alone. However, legally she has the right to be there and has no problems there. Counsel submitted that the minor Claimant will be targeted by Albanian officials because her family supports the Hizmet movement.5

There is no dispute that the Appellant is a citizen of both Albania and Turkey. The starting point for the analysis of a refugee protection claim is that the prospective risk faced by a claimant must be examined against each of the countries where she has citizenship. A refugee protection claimant (Appellant) cannot claim international protection if she can be protected in one of her countries of nationality, in this case, Albania.

On appeal, counsel argues that there was no need for the Appellant, a minor, to make separate allegations in her Basic of Claim (BOC) form given that her case was to have been assessed under her father's BOC.6 But this misses the point. What was incumbent on the Appellant's designated representative and her counsel was to articulate either in her BOC, her parent's BOC, or in the testimony at the hearing, why she faced risk in Albania as a citizen of Albania, as distinct from the rest of the members of her family who only had temporary status in Albania. Which I find was not done.

The Appellant had a designated representative (her father) and legal counsel before the RPD. Her dual nationality as a citizen of both Albania and Turkey was known and not in dispute. Consequently, when completing her BOC form and in providing testimony or other evidence at the hearing, it was open to those assisting her to make a case for her separately against Albania, as an Albanian citizen, either on her BOC form or in a separate paragraph of the parent's BOC form, or in testimony. Indeed, the RPD panel pointed this out at the outset of the hearing. At the opening of the hearing, following a question by the RPD panel, Albania was added by counsel as a country of reference for the Appellant and counsel made a brief submission stating that the Appellant would be persecuted in Albania because of her family membership.7 The matter was raised again by the RPD panel in the hearing during the questioning of the Appellant's father.8

Appellant's counsel asserts on appeal that the minor Appellant's father argued that the family was at risk in both Albania and Turkey, and that the RPD accepted the remainder of the family claims against Albania and Turkey. I disagree. The opening paragraph of the minor Appellant's father's BOC sets out that the fear of persecution or harm is against Turkey.9 The narrative indicates their fear in Albania was in being deported to Turkey given that except for the Appellant, they had only temporary residence status and had been denied citizenship. They also feared the pressures being placed on Albania by Turkish authorities were increasing. However, it does not set out how the minor Appellant, as an Albanian citizen, faced risk in Albania. I note that the RPD decision did not include a finding that the family demonstrated that they faced a serious possibility of persecution or a subsection 97(1) harm if they were to return to Albania. Instead, the RPD only made a finding that the other family member's status in Albania was temporary and that they were not excluded under Article 1E.

I find that initially, as set out in BOCs filed by the family members, the refugee claims of the minor Appellant's family were against Turkey and no other country. I find no record in the recorded testimony of the Appellant's father where he alleged the minor Appellant would be persecuted in Albania as an Albanian citizen. The only direct reference to Albania in the narrative of the minor Appellant's father is the following paragraph below. We also feared for our safety in Albania. We were in fear of abductions by the Turkish authorities due to the connections between Albanian and Turkish Governments like happened in many countries such as recently in Kosovo, Ukraine, Azerbaijan etc. There is nowhere in Turkey where my family and I can live safely. I do not consider this statement to be an allegation of persecution or harm of the minor Appellant Albania as an Albanian citizen.10

I find no error in the RPD's treatment of the evidence in this case including the BOCs, testimony and objective documentation. Counsel for the minor Appellant takes issue with the RPD's examination of a newspaper clipping submitted before the RPD11 that states Albania is part of an international organization that has declared the Hizmet as a terrorist organization. However, on appeal, Appellant's counsel makes no new argument regarding this article. After examining the newspaper clipping and the National Documentation Package (NDP) of Albania, I do not find that either the newspaper clipping referred to by counsel or the NDP establishes that Albanian citizens are being persecuted or harmed in Albania on the basis of their affiliation, or imputed affiliation to Hizmet or because of their family support for Hizmet. The Appellant did not adduce evidence at the RPD or on appeal to demonstrate that Albanian citizens with this profile face a serious risk of persecution or 97(1) harm. I find counsel's argument in this regard to be without merit.

The RPD has focused on the assessment of the prospective risk that the Appellant would face if she were to return from Canada to Albania, one of her countries of citizenship. The RPD concluded that the Appellant, through her father, had not discharged her burden of proof that she would be harmed or persecuted in Albania. I make the same finding. In this regard, it is worth noting the testimony from the designated representative when he was asked to explain the fears he had for his daughter. During the hearing the Appellant's father replied to the RPD panel's questions about his daughter only in regard to the fear of family separation as noted by the RPD in its reasons for decision.12 At the end of the hearing the Appellant's father answered a similar question from his counsel stating that if is daughter were left in Albania alone she could be kidnapped by Turkish agents to force him to return to Turkey.13 I find this evidence to be speculative and I give it little weight. I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err in finding that the burden of proof had not been met. I find that the RPD's conclusion that the minor Appellant is neither a Convention Refugee nor a person in need of protection is correct.

Separation of the family is undoubtedly a problematic situation. However, the RPD and RAD are bound by the legislation and jurisprudence on this matter. In Dawalty,14 the Federal Court states that "there is no concept of family unity incorporated into the definition of Convention refugee ... this Court having chosen to adopt a very narrow view of the definition." In Casetellanos,15 Justice Nadon also ruled in this sense by stating: "The definition of Convention refugee to which Canada subscribes by virtue of its being a signatory to the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees ... does not incorporate the concept of family unity."

It should also be noted that the IRPA does not give the RPD or the RAD the authority to make decisions based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations. However, considering the age of the minor Appellant, I have no doubt that the Minister would give due consideration to her circumstances as the RPD panel also noted at the hearing.16 The role of the RPD, and of the RAD on appeal, is to determine whether there is a serious possibility of persecution for the refugee protection claimant or whether, on a balance of probabilities, she would be subject to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture if she were to return to her country of citizenship. This determination has been made correctly by the RPD and I make the same finding that the minor Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant, XXXX XXXX, is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
